Madam Speaker, since Confederation, and up to 1968, respective Conservative and Liberal Governments respected the rights of individuals to own businesses, land and shares. Under this individual enterprise system, Canada rose to a position of second place in all the world. Individual Canadians were truly free. Since 1968 and the imposition of a government-owned economic system by the Liberal-Socialist Party, Canada has fallen to thirteenth place in OECD and fortieth place in all the world. Individual Canadians are very much less free. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz):
That true Liberal Party supporters across Canada rise up and take control of the Liberal Party and throw out the present Liberal Members who make Lenin and Trotsky look like Genghis Khan.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF INVESTMENT CORPORATION IN VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In British Columbia the verb "to brie" means foolishly to privatize good government corporations with disastrous consequences. Now we fear that the Canada Development Corporation and its invisible Chairman, Anthony Hampson, who pretends to operate out of Vancouver, will lay off 3,250 workers and will privatize or "brie" the Government's 49 per cent share. Further, Senator Jack Austin, the same one who was defeated in Vancouver-Kingsway, has set up the CDIC whose object will be to "brie" Teleglobe, Canadair, de Havil-land and other corporations, with God knows how many layoffs. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper):
That the Government set up a real investment corporation based in Vancouver with a business, labour, and consumer board accountable to an elected Minister of Parliament and with the object of providing jobs, and furthermore, that Messrs. Austin, Bell, Strong and Hampson should be "briced" instead.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PROVINCIAL STATUS FOR YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Today the Minister announced the Government's policy on constitutional development in the Northwest Territories and Yukon. What he did in this announcement was to reject the possibility of provincial status for either the Northwest Territories or Yukon within the foreseeable future. Why has the Government rejected the possibility of provincial status?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PROVINCIAL STATUS FOR YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext: Because the Prime Minister is still alive.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PROVINCIAL STATUS FOR YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the federal Government has rejected anything, it has rejected provincial status now. That is based on realistic factors, such as the tremendous land mass, the limited number of people, and the still relatively narrow economic base.
May I say that our position is based on the realities of the situation. As a northerner himself, I think the Hon. Member knows that there are very few northerners who realistically believe that provincehood, especially in the Territories, is appropriate at this time when they want division. I am talking about the Northwest Territories now. That is a fact. If the Hon. Member is suggesting that they want to wrestle with the question of division now, but want provincehood before that, that seems a ridiculous position and one with which most northerners would never agree.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PROVINCIAL STATUS FOR YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as a northerner I know that people who live in that part of Canada want control of their own affairs, the same as people who live in any other part of the country.

Madam Speaker, my second question deals with the financing of the operation of government in the Territories and in Yukon. At his press conference this morning the Minister rejected the possibility of resource revenue sharing. Instead, he said that it is the policy of the Government to collect all resource revenues and then

November 26, 1982
Oral Questions
hand back dribs and drabs to the Territories as it sees fit. Why has the Minister rejected the possibility of resource revenue sharing?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with reference to the Hon. Member's first remarks, may I say to him that not only the native leadership in the Northwest Territories but also the Executive Committee and the entire Assembly, indicated that they wanted the federal Government to indicate, in principle, its commitment to responsible and politically accountable government in the Territories. That is precisely what we have done and that is, therefore, why I can say with considerable confidence, in terms of the northerners whom 1 have met in the last half hour, that they endorse the Government's policy very enthusiastically. May I indicate that they wished they could have received a similar hearing from the previous Government when they made representations of this kind.
As far as the Hon. Member's question about resource revenue sharing is concerned, may I indicate to him that we met the Territories' desire for formula financing. That will allow them to accept political accountability for the moneys spent in the North. They will make their own decisions with respect to priorities for spending that money. That, again, is the real test of responsible and politically accountable government in the North.
In addition to that, we have established the principle of a discretionary fund that will assure northerners that they will have a fund to offset the cost of development in the North. It is the cost of development that is of particular concern right now.
May I indicate that they wanted the discretionary fund to offset the cost of development because that is where the real problem resides right now. It is exploration that is taking place right now. They are going through a stage of expenditure; there are no revenues, simply mammoth expenditures that must be made in order to attain revenues for the future. That is what we are prepared to share with northerners right now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO AMEND YUKON ACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, may I put a very simple, brief, supplementary question to the Minister. Does he intend to introduce amendments to the Yukon Act which would give Yukon control over its natural resources? Does he intend to introduce similar amendments which would remove his power of veto over elected members of the Legislature introducing measures affecting the expenditure of money?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO AMEND YUKON ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we intend to amend the Yukon Act to give legal basis to the de facto situation which is there now in terms of responsible government. That is a position which the head of the Yukon government wanted us to take for some time, and I suspect that it has the support, not only of that Government but of the Hon. Member himself.
That will take place. In future, also, it will mean that the Governor in Council at the federal Government level will not have to authorize elections. It will be done by the Commission in Council and therefore by the duly elected people in Yukon. Again that is something which is very much desired in the North.
The amendments to the Yukon Act will take place as soon as the claim of the Council for Yukon Indians is settled. In fact, that was the singular condition to us getting ahead with the amendment of that Act. Dennis O'Connor, the negotiator there, a man whom, I believe, the Hon. Member has backed in terms of his tenure as negotiator, indicated with some optimism that that claim will be settled within the next few months. That being the case, I would certainly hope that we could get ahead with the amendments to the Yukon Act, as the Hon. Member has wanted for some time.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING MANDATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. When he announced the formation of the Macdonald Commission it was quite unclear exactly what Mr. Macdonald was going to investigate. In the intervening two or three weeks the whole question has become even more muddled, and yesterday Mr. Macdonald added to the confusion with a press conference. At the press conference he said that he will not give up his corporate directorships-and I assume that applies equally to the other Commissioners-that he will investigate House and Senate reform, that he will take a look at constitutional reform, that he does not know what the Commission will cost, and that in fact he will look into everything with the exception of morality and the state of professional sport in Toronto.
Given that we have a serious economic problem in the country that has to be faced now, could the Prime Minister please tell the House what, in Heaven's name, is this Commission supposed to be doing?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING MANDATE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the clearest answer that I could give the Hon. Member would be to advise him to read the terms of reference which were part of the Order in Council setting up the Commission. If he reads that, he will not only understand what the Commission is intending to do but the Hon. Member will also understand what Mr. Macdonald was saying.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING MANDATE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think I do understand what this is all about, but I am not sure that public funding for Mr. Macdonald's leadership aspirations is a good thing.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING MANDATE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

Madam Speaker, surely the Prime Minister knows that we are already funding-we, the people of Canada-the Science Council and the Economic Council, to look at the future and to determine what kind of economic direction we should be taking. We are
Oral Questions
funding the "blue ribbon committee" to advise the Government on immediate and long-range plans for the economy. Now we are going to spend another $5 million on fees and on advice for this Commission to look into all manner of things, not one single one of which relates directly to current economic conditions and how to solve them.
How can the Prime Minister justify spending $5 million right now on this Commission, given that the Commission hasn't the faintest idea what it is doing, and given that it is duplicating work already being done by other groups funded by the Government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the two "givens" quoted by the Hon. Member are precisely not two "givens". The other work which is done within Government is not work which will be duplicated by this Commission. I repeat it is not a "given" that the Commission does not know what it is going to do. The terms of reference are quite clear. It tells them what they are going to do. The Hon. Member is basing his conclusions and his indignation on two wrong premises. I would urge the Hon. Member to read the terms of reference, and to think with a clear mind of the importance of having Canadians, not part of the Government, looking at the long-term prospects for Canada in economic terms and also in institutional terms.
This is hardly an invention. I had occasion previously when I was questioned to refer to the Rowell-Sirois Commission and to the Gordon Commission, for instance. These were very useful works for the elaboration of thought on the future of Canada, ten, 20, and 30 years down the road. This is what we want to have done outside the partisan atmosphere of this House, outside the more short-term preoccupations of departmental duties.
We want a group of distinguished Canadians, hopefully assisted by large numbers of Canadians in financial, academic and labour circles, who will be able to assist the Commission in arriving at a certain number of principles useful for the guidance of this or any government in orienting Canada toward a progressive path in the future. I repeat this has been done before. It is time that it be done again now, and I would urge the Hon. Member to try to depart a bit from his partisan approach to this and to think of the benefit that can come to Canada from it.
Madam Speaker, it is not a partisan consideration. It was the Prime Minister who appointed Donald Macdonald, not I.
And Romanow.

It was Donald Macdonald who said he wanted to be free to leave and run for the Liberal Party's leadership, not I. If there is any partisanship injected into this, it was the Prime Minister and Donald Macdonald who injected it, not we.

Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member seems to indicate that his mind can only operate at one level. That is not the case with nor is it the duty of the Government which tries to discharge its functions.

subsubtopic: TRAVEL EXPENDITURES OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
The information sought is not readily available from departmental records; only total expenditures are rolled up by Department. Such information would only be available on individual travel claims and would necessitate compilation by hand, the cost of which would far outweigh any informational benefit that might accrue. Departmental emphasis is placed on internal control mechanisms, which require all government business travel to be justified and pre-authorized. Expenditures must be submitted on a travel form, which is compared with the pre-authorization by departmental administration to ensure that proper approval for the trip has been given and that the claimed expenditures comply with those permitted by the travel policy.
A recent survey of travel patterns in a representative sample of seven Departments showed a total of 380,950 trips during 1981-82. In the majority of cases, these are routine trips made by employees involved in direct service to the public, such as weights and measures inspectors, agricultural inspectors and advisers, and health inspectors. The employees generally use their own car or a government car to travel between workplaces during normal working hours. Travel for other reasons, such as travel for business purposes that is not directly related to a regular part of duties, attending conferences or taking training courses, has recently been the subject of more stringent controls by Treasury Board. More specifically, the Board
November 26, 1982

has directed that Departments and agencies reduce business travel that is not directly related to a regular part of duties by 15 per cent from 1981-82 level; foreign travel (which represents 1.6 per cent of all travel) must be approved by the minister responsible, except for trips to continental U.S.A.; and the Minister responsible must also approve conference attendance in excess of two delegates from the Department, as well as all departmental sponsorship of conferences.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-98, an Act to amend the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Madam Speaker, the Canadian horticultural industry is a $3 billion a year business, employing something like 200,000 people. It is a huge and varied industry, stretching from coast to coast. Indeed, it is an international industry. Thanks to the advances that have been made in storage and transportation, our consumers have access to an incredible array of fresh produce from across the country and around the world.
As a matter of fact, Canadians last year imported $1.1 billion worth of fruits and nuts and about $600 million worth of vegetables.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Carleton-Char-lotte (Mr. McCain) rises on a point of order.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is it presumed in this debate that the Minister is now closing the debate, or is he introducing it? Technically, he could be closing it and I wish an opportunity to
speak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: My understanding is that the Minister is proposing a motion to the House, the motion being the Bill. Correct?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Correct. The great distances that fruit and vegetables travel en route to the consumer, coupled with the fact that they are highly perishable products, creates in many instances unique marketing problems. For example, a carload of British Columbia cherries may pull into the Ontario Food Terminal and the buyer is not pleased with the quality. This could be a rare occasion, because most of the time, 99 per cent of the time, the produce from British Columbia is of high quality. But if someone decided to say it was not of that

November 26, 1982
Agricultural Products Standards
quality, and if we did not have a mechanism for arbitrating this kind of problem, the load of cherries would sit there for a long time before some kind of agreement was reached between the buyer and the seller. By then we would have an unholy mess on our hands.
Fortunately, we do have an arbitration mechanism. Unfortunately, that mechanism has not had the legal teeth to do its job effectively since a court challenge to its powers in 1974.
The Arbitration Board has continued to function since then, but without the authority to enforce its rulings. There have, in fact, been cases where a party to a dispute simply refused to pay the amount of compensation which the Board deemed appropriate.
The amendment to the CAPS Act, which is before the House, would clearly establish the Board's legal authority, and would improve some aspects of its operation. I must stress that such action is needed because of the fact that we are dealing with highly perishable goods that are being shipped great distances.
Perhaps I should take a moment to run through the full arbitration procedure, and how the reconstituted board will fit in. First off, everybody who is engaged in the interprovincial and international buying and selling of fruits and vegetables must be licensed by Agriculture Canada. The licensee agrees to obey a code of practice which incorporates normal trading procedures. Here is how the arbitration procedure works. When a buyer feels that the shipment he or she has received is not of the grade requested, or that it has deteriorated in transit, he or she has 24 hours to take exception. Then an official inspection is done by an Agriculture Canada primary products inspector. Next, the buyer contacts the seller to see if they can reach an agreement on the settlement that should be made. If buyer and seller cannot reach an agreement, the seller files a complaint and the matter goes before the Arbitration Board. Meanwhile the buyer is required to dispose of the product to best advantage.
The Arbitration Board has been composed of three experts. The Chairman is appointed by the federal Government and the other two members are representatives from buyers and shippers. When the Board meets, the federal Government pays their per diems. In the reconstituted Board there would be three to five members, appointed by the Minister of Agriculture. Aside from the one or two Government representatives, the industry members would be nominated by the trade associations. As with the old system, the Board's decisions can be referred to a Board of Review. The old Board included the original members of the Arbitration Board, plus the Department's legal adviser and the director of our dairy, fruit and vegetable division. The new Board of Review will not include members who sat on the Arbitration Board.
Under the proposed system, the Board of Review will only be able to review how the Arbitration Board made its ruling; whether it considered all the information. From there, if the buyer or seller is still dissatisfied, and refuses to pay the amount recommended by the Board, the Board's decision is
passed on to the Federal Court, and in effect becomes a decision of the court.
The Minister of Agriculture also has some scope to help ensure the smooth operation of the Board. The Minister has the authority to revoke the licence of a party that refuses to abide by the rulings of the Board, or who is the subject of repeated complaints. It is important to note that the procedure I have just outlined is followed by most of our fruit and vegetable trading partners, most notably the United States. It is only reasonable that we should be able to provide a reciprocal service to settle international disputes.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the long-overdue amendments I am proposing will help in the orderly marketing of agricultural products. As you and the Members of this House know, agriculture is prone to such an incredible range of production and marketing hazards, it is only reasonable that we should try to reduce some of the element of risk through the provision of a good arbitration service so as to make it fair and operate in a very smooth fashion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some eight years ago there was a ruling of the court which said that the establishment and rulings of the Arbitration Board for purposes outlined by the Minister were ultra vires and not binding. I think it would have been very important for the Minister to tell us in what way he has now closed the gate so that producers, dealers and receivers will now be able to get a reasonable, binding decision with respect to a dispute. Looking at this Bill and its predecessor, I wonder why the first one was thrown out and why this one will not be thrown out under the circumstances.
The absence, Mr. Speaker, of binding authority has been a very serious situation, and the Canadian Fruit Wholesalers Association and the Canadian Horticultural Council, the two groups which in the main represent the shipper and receiver of fresh fruits and vegetables, have been pressing very hard to have this system re-established. One of the real difficulties which arose was the fact that people who shipped into Canada really had no means of obtaining a settlement of a problem which might arise. One may ship a product in top-flight condition but in some cases it may arrive in less favourable condition. As a result there is often a dispute which arises between the shipper and receiver, and we need this Board of Arbitration to sit down around the table with the parties concerned and arrive at a binding decision. However, such a vehicle has not been available.
In the U.S., if such a situation arose, there is a vehicle of comparable nature which would arbitrate the dispute. Once the ruling is made, the licence of the person against whom the decision is made is in jeopardy if the claim is not in fact paid. American shippers of these goods into our markets have found themselves unable to obtain a reasonable, binding solution upon a customer in Canada who may wish to abuse the foreign shipper. The result has been that the American association has decreed that any Canadian involved in a dispute must post a
November 26, 1982

bond equal to twice the amount of the claim lodged. This has caused some very serious difficulties for Canadians who ship their produce into the American market.
It has worked both ways, Mr. Speaker. The shippers from outside this country are uncertain as to their legal status with respect to the produce they ship into Canada, and people shipping out of Canada into the United States find themselves in a very difficult position when they attempt to make a claim concerning an unsatisfactory deal in the United States. So it is high time that a procedure to settle these problems is in fact in place. Trade between our two countries has suffered and American publications such as The Packer, which some people call the bible of the wholesale fruit and vegetable industry in the U.S., have been levying charges at Canada which are not very complimentary. So the earlier this Bill is in place, the earlier we can re-establish our historic relationship with the American receivers of our goods as well as the American shippers of our needs, the more healthy will be the trade between the two countries.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that this present situation has affected all sorts of agricultural trade between Canada and the U.S. It is being used as a weapon. For example, in the potato disagreement between Canada and the U.S., particularly the State of Maine, the Americans are saying that Canada does not deal in good faith any more. They do not want to deal with us. The situation is giving us a reputation which we can ill afford. It is therefore imperative that this Bill should pass, be given Royal Assent and proclaimed at a reasonably early date.
Fortunately, during that period in which a legal and binding Board could not be established by the Department of Agriculture, an Acting Board has been the arbiter of disputes between shippers and receivers of fresh fruit and vegetable products. Its decisions were not binding but in roughly 75 per cent of cases they were accepted. However, even though a shipper may have been found at fault by the existing Arbitration Board, his licence is not in jeopardy. The decisions of the Acting Board do not have the weight that the Bill would give the appointed Board.
1 suppose the Minister could suspend a licence if he chose to do so, but so far he has not. The proposed legislation gives the Minister the authority to issue or cancel a licence. I think the circumstances under which a licence could be suspended should be defined. The Bill is not clear on this point although it may be set out in the regulations which will follow.
Having just attended a seminar on fisheries, I feel it is imperative that the House, the Committee and the trade should know the terms and conditions under which licences are to be granted. It has been suggested that any dealer in the fresh fruit and vegetable trade should submit a bond with his application for a licence. This would put pretty serious constraints upon free access to business. I would say that probably the three largest dealers in fruit and vegetables today started with a roadside stand. They have managed their businesses in
Agricultural Products Standards
such a way as to gain the confidence of the trade and so have become very large indeed.
If we are going to insist on a bond, it should be available at a reasonable cost. There may, of course, be cases where someone with a bad reputation in the trade applies for a licence but cannot provide an adequate bond. In the main, however, the amount of the bond should not be so high as to act as a constraint.
The same remarks apply to licencing. If the cost of the licence is prohibitive, it is a constraint upon entry into this kind of business. I know that representations have been made for a large licence fee which would act as a constraint to entry into the business, but I think this should be considered very seriously. Until it is proven that irresponsible people are entering the business, excessive constraints should not be imposed.
There is a technical matter that concerns me, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the Minister will address it. As I understand it, no constraint is imposed upon one farmer who ships products to another farmer. On the other hand, if a difficulty about the shipment should arise, there would not be access to the Board of Arbitration. Should we not consider imposing a nominal licence fee for producers and purchasers? 1 think both should be licensed prior to the product being inspected at point of origin or at destination. Some people in this category do quite a little bit of business on their own and I think they should have an element of protection.
The seed potato industry is an example of this. There is really no way that a farmer in one province can know the financial reliability or integrity of someone who receives his product. An element of protection should be afforded such people.
There are some other aspects of the legislation that I should like to discuss, Mr. Speaker. It provides for a Board of "not less than three and not more than five members", but does not set out any guidelines for the qualifications of members. Perhaps that will be provided for in the regulations. The Minister touched on that matter this morning but not as fully as I should have liked. The explanatory note provides that the Bill would:
(b) empower the Governor in Council to make regulations, including regulations prescribing the products for which a licence is required and standards for those products-
This would mean an overlapping of regulations, because there already is a standard for grades of fruit and vegetables shipped within this country. Now we are proposing to regulate in respect of grade, standards, packages and other items. I should like the Minister to explain this overlapping of regulations when the Bill goes to Committee.
It occurs to me that licensed dealers in Canada should have the Arbitration Board available to them at the federal level for sales within a province. They would be licensed to ship products dealer to dealer under federal standards. In some Provinces there is a mechanism for dealing with problems that may arise, but in others there is no such provision. I do not think it would be an infringement upon provincial jurisdiction if there were an opportunity for licensed dealers to approach this

November 26, 1982
Agricultural Products Standards
Arbitration Board to settle disputes which might arise from shipments made within a Province.
I am quite concerned about the qualifications of people appointed to the Board and about its status, Mr. Speaker. Clause 1, amending Section 6 of the Act, reads as follows:
6.2 (3). The Board is a court of record and shall have an official seal, which shall be judicially noticed.
That does not mean a great deal to the man on the street, Mr. Speaker, and it does not mean as much to me as it would to a lawyer, but I can see that it gives the Board a high status.
Clause 1, amending Section 6.6 of the Act, provides that the Board will have full jurisdiction. Appeal from its decisions may be made under Section 28 of the Federal Court Act. I do not know what is contained in that Section but I am advised that the Arbitration Board and the Appeal Board, known as the Tribunal, can rule on the fate of an individual without that individual having access to the courts of appeal. Apparently if someone were to appeal as provided in this Clause, he would find that the court has very little scope for action and would be virtually unable to reverse the Board's decision unless there was a great error in judgment or some aspect of the law. I do not know whether this really affects the human rights of individuals in Canada under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but I think the constraints of appeal to the courts of Canada are too excessive.
I reflect again upon the qualifications of the individuals who will constitute these Boards. As I understand it, they will not be legal minds. Nor do I think in the initial adjudication of a problem should they be legal minds. I think they should be minds which are knowledgeable of situations that can occur in the trade and that their decisions should be based upon them. When one fails to extend the full right of the courts of Canada to traders, I submit that that is precluding the opportunity for legal interpretation. Whether it may go for or against the appellant is really not the factor which should be considered. It is the fact that he cannot effectively get to the court to try to appeal a decision which he feels is unjust.
There is no clear indication in the Act as to what it may cost the individual to take his case to the Arbitration Board. I wish that could be defined. I think it is imperative for the sake of the trade that one in fact knows what will be the cost. I presume the cost will be spelled out by regulation, and I ask the Minister to give his attention to this item as well.
Referring to Section 6.7(2)(c) dealing with people who handle agricultural products on commission, I should like to ask whether they will be licensed as dealers or brokers. This is a question which must be addressed. At the present time I believe that the broker, the intermediary between buyer and seller, is not subject to the Arbitration Board except on very, very rare occasions. Since we are looking at the word "commission" as used in the Section to which I have referred, I raise the question as to whether or not brokers will in fact be subject to decisions of and responsible for the decisions of an arbitration case which happened to be put before the Board.
I do not have any intention of suggesting that this Bill is not needed. I do not have any intention of suggesting that this Party will block it. If the regulations are reasonable, if the Minister's answers are explanatory and address the questions I have raised today, I think we could expect that in the haste required this Bill could be put through.
I do ask the Minister to make a change in practice in the House, one which is very rarely observed. I think the Standing Committee on Agriculture should have an opportunity to study the regulations section by section, because his regulatory power is so broad. I think the Canadian Horticultural Council, the Canadian Fruit Wholesalers Association and any other group or organization within the trade itself should have an opportunity to express themselves in respect of the regulations, and I think the committee should have the benefit of that. I do not believe that the regulations and regulatory power extended to the Minister under the Act should be exercised without advance warning and without consideration by the committee. Some of the committee Members, including the Hon. Member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne), are familiar with the practice of the trade and how the regulations will or will not work. I want them to look at the regulations, particularly because I do not want overlapping. I do not want consumer legislation and agricultural legislation in the regulatory structure interfering one with the other. We have troubles enough now without that. If we are to get into packaging as mentioned in the Act, then let us know that other Act will regulate packaging, labelling, etc.
I have nothing further to say. I look forward to discussing the Bill in committee. I hope it can be done quickly because the Act is needed for the benefit of the trade; it is needed very badly and post haste.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today is one which the horticultural industry and the fruit and vegetables industry have been awaiting for some time. Since 1974 they have been operating under a procedure which does not have any form of legality; it is strictly a voluntary type of operation. This has created some problems for fruit and vegetable producers in international markets.
The Bill is designed to reimplement an arbitration procedure which was in place and well understood prior to 1974. It will apply to shippers and wholesalers or producers of fruit and vegetables both in interprovincial and international trade. It is well known in the House but perhaps less known to the general public that agricultural trade in any product within a province is within the jurisdiction of the Province, and that the rules and regulations for the conduct of trade are handled within each Province. Each of the ten Provinces have their own ways and means of ensuring that buyers and sellers are adequately treated. Basically, the Bill is to apply to interprovincial trade and to trade between Canada and the United States and Canada and other countries.
I suppose pressure for the change has been present for some time. A court case challenging the voluntary arbitrary procedure occurred in 1974. It was a case involving a Montreal
November 26, 1982

wholesaler and retailer. Since that time the arbitration procedure has been open to challenge. This is the first time the Government has seen fit to formalize the procedure which existed then.
Basically, the Bill proposes to set up a Board of five members to do two things. First, it will licence people engaged in importation, exportation or interprovincial trade in any agricultural product which is defined for the purposes of the Act as fruit or vegetables. Second, any question of grade or quality of goods delivered or received will be handled in the following manner: the local Government grader will be called in to determine whether the grades described on the manifest or in the agreement between the two parties were indeed the actual grades and whether the products were the quality they were alleged to be. If there is still a dispute, there is an attempt to arbitrate it by the officials; if that fails, it goes to a Board.
This five-member Board of Arbitration will be set up with its head office in the National Capital Region, according to Bill C-98. The Board members will be appointed for a term not to exceed five years, but at the pleasure of the Minister he can drop the Board members at any time, which is fairly standard in these types of operations. As well, Board members are eligible for reappointment if they have done a good job.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Or continue to vote the right way.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
As my colleague has just said, or continue to vote the right way.
There are standard procedures on how to handle this situation if all the members are not there. The Bill states that a quorum shall consist of a minimum three members. It provides that members of the Board may hear cases in any part of Canada. It does not, however, set out who the members of the Board shall be, from what industry, or from what regions they should come. I assume that decision will be left either to ministerial discretion or be spelled out by regulation. I think the trade would prefer it be spelled out a little more clearly, but we can get into that matter during the hearings of the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
Unlike some of the Bills we have dealt with, there is no requirement for a notice of meeting. It says only that three members of the Board constitute a quorum. There is nothing about how much time members of the Board shall have of notice of a meeting. This may be an important point, given the nature of the country. Canada is a far-flung country consisting of five different time zones. Some members of the Board may, in fact, need a day or more than a day's notice in order to fly to the National Capital Region, or to wherever the meeting is called. That is a point that should be considered. Perhaps during our committee hearings we might decide whether giving notice of a meeting should be set out in the Bill itself or whether it is something that could be dealt with adequately by regulation.
Agricultural Products Standards
The procedures for laying down complaints are outlined in the Bill. They are not terribly direct; they provide some variation. The Bill simply states that where the goods delivered or received do not meet the standards, within nine months after the Board has been made aware that one or other of the parties is dissatisfied with the goods, the Board shall have dealt with the case or have been provided with a written complaint. Some complaints with which the Board will be dealing will be fairly ancient by the time they reach the Board. But the complainants must file a written complaint. That is suitable. This procedure will not cost either of the complainants a great deal of money and, according to my reading of the Bill, people will have nine months to file such complaint. That seems to me to be a good long time for the process to get off the ground.
As previous speakers have mentioned, the Board has a fair amount of power. It is considered to be a court or record and its decisions will be judicially noted. The Board, as a court of record, is empowered to call witnesses if necessary and to swear them in. This Board is, in fact, vested with all the powers, rights and privileges that are vested in a superior court of record. It can issue summonses requiring people to appear before it and requiring either producers or receivers of goods to provide any and all records that apply to the subject matter at hand.
The powers of this Board are fairly substantial. It can also receive such evidence as the Board itself considers to be relevant, trustworthy and credible to the case.
The decisions of this Board will be treated as final, the same as any court of record. The Board must list its reasons for arriving at a decision. The aggrieved parties may then appeal to a Board of Review. Probably there will be very little action in court that can be taken outside of these two forums that will be available to producers and receivers of goods. The review tribunal will consist of five members, three of whom must be available to hear any case brought before it. It appears that this will be a sort of supreme court in Canada for agricultural products and standards applied thereto.
This review tribunal's office is to be located in the National Capital Region. The duties of its members are very similar to those of the Board, with the exception that it is to be a higher court providing appeal privileges. This particular group can hear any appeal. The grievance must be filed within 30 days after the Board has reached its decision. The tribunal basically has three choices. It can affirm the finding of the Board; it can vary or cancel the decision; or it can make another decision. The procedures are outlined fairly clearly. However, I have a bit of trouble with the procedure laid down, not with what is stated in the Bill but with what is left out.
As I read the Bill, the only power the Board or the tribunal has to implement findings would be the possibility of lifting the licence which the parties involved have received from the Ministry of Agriculture. That is the only punitive action that can be taken against someone who is found to have delivered faulty products. There is no bonding provision. There is no way of protecting the aggrieved party. I think this is a reasonably

November 26, 1982
Agricultural Products Standards
serious short coming in the Bill which will have to be dealth with by amending the Bill. I hope Government Members will be presenting such an amendment; this omission has been brought to their attention. If they do not present an amendment, I hope Government Members will see fit to support an amendment from the Opposition side of the House. I am prepared to move an amendment dealing with the bonding provision, which I think should be included since the aggrieved party has no financial protection the way the Bill is framed at present.
I think it is quite necessary it should do so because one of the problems that has been outlined to us by producers and handlers of fruits and vegetables, particularly on an international basis, is the difficulties they have going into American markets. American buyers have become rather leery of dealing with Canadian products because our laws do not provide any means for settling disputes.
This Bill will change that situation. Until now, United States buyers have been demanding a bond in value equal to twice the value of every shipment that enters the United States. This bonding requirement is punitive to Canadian exporters. We in this Party believe that the bonding provision could be an integral part of the Bill and would lower the cost of bonding to those involved in the fruit and vegetables industry to make them equally competitive with U.S. producers.
We believe that this legislation is important to the entire industry, especially since the fruit and vegetables sector has great room for expansion. Canada still imports a vast amount of fruits and vegetables which our climate is capable of growing. For example, in 1981 we imported $2.8 million worth of frozen broccoli which we are capable of growing and freezing in this country. We imported $875,00 worth of frozen peas which can even be grown in the Yukon. We imported approximately $2.9 million of frozen carrots and $1.4 million in frozen spinach. Other assorted frozen vegetables were imported in the amount of $4.7 million. A great many of these products could be produced in this country and frozen here in our freezing industry. The only possible reason we are not producing these products ourselves is that the industry has not been given the support which could make it viable.
The amount of fresh produce which is imported causes greater concern. While we obviously need to import bananas and other tropical fruits, we import other fruits which we could easily grow in this country. For instance, $92.4 million worth of tomatoes are imported annually. We have a greenhouse industry in Canada which is attempting to meet some of that domestic demand, but this is being hampered to some extent by the Government's taxation policy on natural gas. Greenhouses use mainly natural gas as a source of heat during the winter months. There are, however, other heating options which have not been totally utilized. For example, on the Prairies, where I come from, the climate is much colder than in southern Ontario where most of the greenhouse industry is located, but there are greenhouses on the Prairies which
function year round. They are built next to power stations which simply release their excess heat into the atmosphere. Experiments have been conducted by building greenhouses beside these stations to allow the warm air to flow in between two layers of plastic and glass to heat the air inside the greenhouse. The tomatoes and cucumbers which are being grown in these greenhouses are selling locally at a very great premium compared to what is being imported during the winter from southern California and Mexico. People find these products delicious and are willing to pay 50 per cent to 100 per cent more for them. These products are so popular that people check with the produce department in anticipation of a new shipment. These products are gone from the shelves soon after they have been offered. The only problem is that not enough is being produced now.
Another example of a product which is imported but can be grown here is potatoes. We import almost $44 million worth per year. As well, we import $36 million worth of onions. We import over $30 million worth of cabbage, broccoli and asparagus. Approximately $40 million worth of green beans, carrots and cauliflower is imported and over $30 million worth of celery. Another big import item is lettuce , of which almost $68 million worth was imported. Again, this is a product which can be grown in greenhouses. Green peppers are another potential greenhouse product. There was $17 million worth of cucumbers imported into Canada.
There are certain areas of our country where the agricultural potential could be expanded. For example, $75 million worth of apples and pears are imported annually when the Maritimes could expand the production of tree fruits. There are certain parts of New Brunswick where grain production has been declining because of the wet climate. However, those areas are suitable for growing pears and apples. These areas which have that potential should be encouraged to increase the production of soft fruits in order to provide more jobs and increase the self-sufficiency of the entire country.
We hope that this Bill will provide increased inspection services at urban markets. Many of the expanding urban centres in our country do not have the proper market facilities where this inspection service can take place. It is time for terminal markets to be established with the assistance of the provincial and federal Governments. This would make the service available to producers, wholesalers and retailers.
We are prepared to have this Bill go to committee. I suggest it is important that the Government bring in the amendments I have suggested with respect to bonding in the committee. As well, we would be interested to hear some of the Government's proposals with respect to regulations. We hope that these will be discussed in the committee and that the Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary will provide us with a full description of the type of regulations which they envisage being included in the Bill so we may better understand their position.
May I call it one o'clock?

It seems to me that there is a wide variety of sizes of businesses operating in this realm. Some do several hundred thousands of dollars worth of business in a year while others do business amounting to millions of dollars. Shipments that some businesses handle in a week amount to one or two truckloads while other companies handle several truckloads. The size of the bond in each case would have to be consistent with the size of the business which is operating. This could be worked out in discussions between the two parties, the Horticultural Council and the wholesalers group.
I would hope that the Department of Agriculture and the Board which will be set up by this legislation would have discussions to arrive at a consensus among these groups so that it will be possible for several levels of bonds to exist and for a small firm to grow. The bonding provision should not be seen as a detriment to business. As well, those kinds of discussions should occur prior to the final regulations setting the amount of licence fees, because we do not want to see the licence
Agricultural Products Standards
proving to be a detriment to anyone going into the fruit and vegetable trades.
I therefore close with a final plea that the Government provide an adequate bonding regulation in the amendments during the committee process. We are prepared to support that aspect in principle, as well as the Bill; but we will be raising the kinds of questions and concerns 1 have described in my remarks this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to a conclusion the debate on Bill C-98, which is entitled an Act to amend the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act. As has been previously mentioned, all Parties in the House of Commons are generally in agreement with the Bill.
This is basically a housekeeping Bill. It sets down the guidelines under which a Minister of Agriculture can operate and under which the new Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act will, in effect, operate. We all look forward to this Bill being brought before the committee. The committee will have an opportunity to review the licensing, bonding and cancellation of licences. We will be able to review them in relation to the existing horticultural industry.
The legislation has been requested for some eight years. Finally, we are getting these amendments. However, we are getting them without the regulations that are normally attached to a Bill such as this. The regulations is one area we will want to look at in committee.
The Bill defines "dealer" as any person engaged in the business of purchasing or selling agricultural products. That is a rather wide scope. We hope some dealers will come to Ottawa to appear before our committee. The Bill requires dealers who engage in the importation or exportation of fruits and vegetables, or interprovincial trade in those products, which is trade between the Provinces in this country, to hold a licence to be issued for the purpose as described in the Bill. That licence will be issued by the Minister of Agriculture. This is one requirement in the legislation.
The second part of the legislation would empower the Governor in Council to make regulations, including regulations describing the products for which a licence is required. The Bill describes agricultural products as any fresh fruit or vegetable. That again is a wide range. The Bill would empower the Government to make regulations for the fruit and vegetables industry. This industry has been calling for such a move for some time.
The Bill would establish a Board of Arbitration to hear complaints against licensed dealers from, I assume, affected parties. The Board would hear complaints regarding the failure to comply with the prescribed standards that we hope to discuss at some length in the Agriculture Committee. This is

November 26, 1982
Agricultural Products Standards
done in other countries such as the United States, our largest customer. It is a step in the right direction.
The last amendment to the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act would be to establish a review tribunal to which application may be made for a review of a decision of the Board. That is a stop-gap or safety valve measure. In other words, if a party is not satisfied with the Board of Arbitration ruling, it can move to a review tribunal.
One area we will want to look at in dealing with this legislation is the regulations. While this is a move in the right direction, we do not want to get into a situation where the industry is over-regulated. I do not believe that will be a problem with the five-man group to be set up to look into the matters I have outlined. Nevertheless, that is always a concern for the agricultural industry. While the industry wants help from the Government from time to time, it does not want to be over-regulated, something that seems to be inherent in much of what the Government does.
We look forward to dealing with the legislation in committee from the point of view of making the amendments more workable and to bring this Act up to date. Hopefully our work will attract some attention in the press. When dealing with the legislation, we will want to look at the horticultural industry which makes a tremendous contribution to this country in terms of food, processing and employment.
A number of people in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes, and to a lesser extent, although increasingly, in western Canada, are employed in the horticultural industry. As far as employment is concerned, it is probably one of the largest components in the agricultural industry. From time to time the industry has felt that it has been left out with regard to how it feels the Government should operate. Over the years, it does not feel it has had protection against dumping from other countries. One such example is apples.
At the time when the marketing of apples is almost over in the United States, the picking and selling of apples in British Columbia is just starting. If the Americans have a large crop, they may get rid of the tail end of that crop by shipping it out of the country at a fire sale price. This has happened not only with apples but with other commodities. It has happened in almost every region of this country. The horticulture industry has cried foul, and rightly so. I urge the Government to do something in terms of temporary tariff protection.
I want to make a few comments about tariff protection. There is an ugly scenario developing at this time in connection with the whole question of tariffs in international trade which could have a direct impact on agriculture, specifically in the horticulture industry. I am afraid we are moving dangerously close to an all-out trade war in 1983. This is happening for a number of reasons. The main reason is that the economy in countries around the world is in poor shape. When that occurs, countries have a tendency to retrench and throw up barriers to
protect their producers from products of other countries. The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade meeting at the present time is attempting to deal with that question. We made some gains in terms of freer trade at the Tokyo Round in 1978. Nevertheless, this menace to world trade and our standard of living is a real possibility.
The horticultural industry could get hurt very badly if this is allowed to happen. 1 hope that is going to be one of the areas we are going to be able to discuss with the horticultural industry in the Agriculture Committee because it is probably their biggest single uncertainty at the present time.
In conclusion, we are looking forward to dealing with this legislation from the point of view of seeing if we can make it more responsive to the industry's needs, if in fact they want it changed-and there is some understanding there will be some changes made; but more importantly to have a good discussion and to have the Canadian public and the Members of the Agriculture Committee get a better understanding, a better feel and a better direction for one of the most important industries in this country, the horticultural industry.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take a great deal of time in this debate because I expect that my friend who represents a lot of agriculturists in Vancouver-Kingsway would like to speak, so I will not unduly delay the House with my remarks on this agricultural topic.
I represent a riding that is partially urban and partially rural. Agriculture is a very important industry in my riding. We have many farms on which people work full-time, if they can, but most of the time they are unable to do so as they are required by the nature of their income to take other part-time jobs. So while we have a substantial number of full-time farmers, we have an even larger number of part-time agriculturists.
The main crops in my riding are such things as broccoli, cabbage, strawberries and various other kinds of small fruits. The horticultural products that could be grown there are not grown, for a variety of reasons that have been touched on by previous speakers.
That has not always been the case. When I was growing up my family depended for its income upon a cannery. It was called Canadian Canners; later on it was bought out by American interests, as so much of our canning industry has been in Canada. The Hon. Member from southern Ontario knows that the food processing industry and the preserving industry in Canada is now largely American-owned. I think the only major one that is left in Canada is Canada Packers. We know what happened to Aylmer; it was bought out I believe by Del Monte. We have Stokely-Van Camp and jolly Green Giant and a number of other American firms who are
November 26, 1982

operating in business as part of the multinational food industry or agri-business industry in this country.
My hon. friend from Saskatoon reads to us these horror stories about the amounts of imports that are available in Canada, chiefly from the United States: frozen broccoli, nearly $3 million worth; frozen peas, which we can grow in abundance in many parts of Canada, almost $1 million worth; frozen carrots, nearly $3 million worth; frozen spinach, $1.4 million worth; and all kinds of frozen vegetables as well as the fresh produce which has come to us from our good friends from California, other Southern states and Mexico, are imported.
We had hoped that if there were any beneficial results from the higher energy costs, it would be the fact that importing food would be a good deal more expensive because of the transportation costs and more Canadian produce would be acceptable in our markets because of its competitive price.
When one looks at these figures dealing with cabbage, potatoes, broccoli and tomatoes, 1 know whole areas of the country that used to produce these commodities but no longer do so. I wonder what is the matter with us, as Canadians? We have allowed not only our preserving industry to be sold out, but, along with that, because we have sold out our canneries- there used to be about ten of them in the Province of British Columbia-it follows that the producers of those commodities have gone out of business to because there was no market for their product. As a consequence, all Canadians have suffered. We have become much more dependent on imported products, and if we import products it certainly does not produce a great deal in terms of jobs.
Some people will counter by saying that the consumer got a break by importing these products. I am not sure that that is the case. If we become so dependent on imported products that we no longer have any agricultural industry in our country, including in my own riding, I think what will happen is that we could get an ultimatum to the effect that we will have to export our water to satisfy U.S. needs in the irrigation areas that produce all these fruits and vegetables, or we will be deprived of those imports when we need them.
What we need to do is to look at ways, in an agricultural strategy, to enhance these industries, rather than let them dwindle and erode to the point where there is nothing left.
I could go on and list all the products that we used to grow. Was there a part of this that the Hon. Member missed that he would like me to repeat? I would like to name just one. Once upon a time the area that I represent, and those areas contiguous to it, produced all kinds of fresh strawberries and we had the capacity to freeze them. I understand that last year we imported something like $31 million worth of fresh strawberries. That is absolutely ludicrous. Since we have an area that can produce small fruits or soft fruits, to import $8 million or $9 million worth of frozen strawberries, I think is shameful. At the same time we have nearly two million people unemployed.

Some people are quick to say yes, but they won't pick strawberries. The point is that they will and they do.
One of the things that I would like to congratulate the Government for is the changes in the unemployment insurance regulations, Section 16, which allow for the first time agricultural workers who work only a very few days at any one farm to add them up in order to qualify for the 28 days. Previous to that change by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), many of these people who worked on these farms in the Lower Mainland, and also in parts of my riding, have been forced into the arms of labour contractors in order to qualify for unemployment insurance. Many of us who are very quick to criticize the Government should be equally alert to opportunities to state publicly when a good job has been done in a particular area, in response to representations, to let people know that we appreciate that.
Getting back to strawberries, one of the reasons we are in difficulty in Canada in terms of fresh produce imports-and this was touched on by the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta)-is the fact that because we are a northern country we are seasonally disadvantaged. When there is a surplus at the end of the season, in some places to the south of us, such as the United States, their price goes down and offers are made to the large supermarkets in this country through brokers at a price which is much lower than the price for our production, which is just coming into its peak. While it is not technically dumping, and therefore the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has no right to intervene, it does of necessity destroy the value of our crops that are coming into peak production. Even the offer for sale of a particular commodity which competes with the domestic product is enough to drive our prices down. I can give the examples of strawberries, apricots and peaches, things that we produce extremely well in our country. That is one of the problems we have, which applies not only to the preservation or canning industry we once had, but also to the fresh produce industry.
Anyway, while I think the Bill can be supported, I would also like to express a long-standing concern over the fact that, as in so many other industries in this country, we have allowed our capacity to be eroded; and if there was ever a time when we needed to look to a change in direction to reverse this trend, which goes back almost a generation, I would think the time is now.
I do not think we should try to hold up this measure too long. This Bill is designed to implement arbitration procedures between producers, shippers and wholesalers in interprovincial and international trade. At present, and since 1974, no such arbitration exists, I am told, because of a court case in 1974 which resulted in the old legislation being declared ultra vires. The Horticultural Council and the Canadian Food Wholesalers Association have been trying ever since to have it reinstated. Thirdly, I think it is causing problems for shippers to the United States because we do not have an Act which allows
November 26, 1982

recourse for buyers in the United States. As a result, U.S. buyers are demanding, in the case of disputes, a bonding of 200 per cent of the value of the shipment. That, of course, makes it difficult for our industry and we should take steps to change that situation. The Bill will require that the buyer and seller both be bonded in order to obtain a licence. A refusal to submit to bonding will result in the licence being lifted. This will put teeth into the Act and ensure that all parties are protected and are required to deal in good faith.
