Rather than bemoan that present economic structures are leading us towards ruin-
This is what the Government is always saying about us in the Opposition; perhaps it should listen. He continued:
we should seize opportunities to reverse the trend and make ourselves more self-sufficient-at an individual or community level.
This is what the committee should take into consideration when it is discussing the horticultural industry.
Some people say that the Bill before the House is not important, that it is just a matter dealing with Canadian agricultural products and that we should let the farmer representatives in the House speak on it. I do not agree. This is why I am speaking today. I think people from urban ridings should heed the message of Richard Kadulski and his words of wisdom.
We need more federal inspectors to mediate any disputes under the Act and to ensure top quality products for consumers. Also farm markets should be encouraged and growers assisted to meet demand as it grows. One of the good things the Government has done over the past few years was to
encourage the expansion of a fantastic farmer's market on Granville Island in Vancouver. It has just caught on. Local produce, as much as is possible, is coming to that market. When the committee discusses agricultural standards and deals with Clause 1 of the Bill with reference to licensing, the inspection provisions of the Bill, the Boards and the marketing, the people appointed to the Boards, the appeals of particular decisions and so on, it should consider the new urban markets. I say this because "agricultural product" under the Bill means any fresh fruit or vegetable and the word "dealer" is defined later in the Bill.
There are some people in my riding who actually operate in the farmers' market on Granville Island. I congratulate the people who had something to do with getting it going. I make the point that terminal markets should be encouraged in more urban centres in Canada.
I was serious when I referred to the use of energy sources. I remember being in Regina and being shown by two university professors how they had grown tomatoes around a pipeline. They showed us these tomatoes. They were not the rubbery ones which one purchases in Safeway or other supermarkets. They were really good tomatoes. This is an example of what could be developed as a spin-off from such a Canadian industry. Anyone who has lived in Yellowknife, as I did for a couple of years, has gone to the supermarket there and seen the tremendous cost of food, especially fresh vegetables and fruit, and often frozen foods. I think the north could use some of the spin-offs from our energy power for such greenhouses in which to grow produce.
Finally, I should like to refer to a friend of mine who immigrated from Korea to the Fraser Valley in the Richmond Delta area. He had invented a movable greenhouse. He was able to plant his crop, and because the crops are quite early there, he was able to plant a couple of them. When a crop was finished, he would move the greenhouse in order to plant another crop and so on. It is a little invention, but it indicates the imagination of many Canadians in various walks of life, whether it is in the greenhouse industry, in tomatoes, in the Energex Conference or urban markets. We can do anything we want in Canada even though we are a cold country. I think we can cut down on the imports of such produce as broccoli, tomatoes and so on.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intervene in this debate particularly because of Subsections 6.2 and 6.7, among other things. There was a famous exchange in the British Parliament when Winston Churchill extended the rationing of coal and fish in Great Britain during the War. Nye Bevan rose in response and said, "Mr. Speaker, England is an island of coal surrounded by a sea of fish, and only the organizational genius of the Right Honourable gentleman could see to it that we had a shortage of both".
November 26, 1982

Similarly, Canada is a country full of grain, with many bakers and bakery workers. Only the organizational genius of the Government could see to it that we are using American grain to make buns in the United States, to be brought up to Canada for sale through an outfit called McDonald's. This is an example of what has happened for a long time in the Canadian food chain, from the producer to the consumer. Consequently, it is an example of how the ability of Canadian producers to provide Canadians with more production has been reduced. Mainly it has gone into the hands of producers of fruit, vegetables, grain and grain products in the United States.
If, as and when we have to import fresh fruit and vegetables, surely Canada should be concentrating on importing from countries which definitely need the benefit of the export trade-and I am thinking of countries such as Mexico, and those in the Caribbean and Central America-rather than relying on the producers of fruit, vegetables, grain and grain products in the United States, mostly owned and controlled by oligopolies or whatever in the food production, processing, transportation, wholesaling and retailing business.
If I could illustrate, an agriculture product is a grain product, or vice versa. Let me illustrate what is happening to trade in British Columbia. In 1967-1968 British Columbia imported $1 million worth of bread and bakery products from the United States and exported $2.3 million worth of those products. By last year, 1980-1981, British Columbia was exporting $300,000 worth of bread and bakery products while importing from the United States $11.8 million worth. That is what has happened in that brief period of time from 1967 to 1981, a span of 15 years. Not only has there been a reversal in trade, but it has been a reversal in the order of ten times in dollar figures.
The same thing applies to production, processing-particularly processing-and the wholesaling of fruit and vegetable products. Much of the goods produced in Canada are canned and processed south of the forty-ninth parallel. Again, only the organizational genius of this Government could see to it that we had a shortage of processing capability in Canada for the food products that we produce ourselves.
It is not just some narrow nationalism or protectionism that I am talking about, I am talking about our failure to meet much more of Canada's needs by Canadian producers and processors.
Canadian producers are being victimized by fire sale grain prices in the United States. As a result, Canadian flour costs 45 per cent more in Vancouver than it does in Seattle.
Now look at what has happened. McDonald's wants to import buns. McDonald's restaurants cancelled their contracts with McGavin's bakery. Forty-four jobs were lost in British Columbia, 19 in Manitoba and 11 in Saskatchewan. What did
Agricultural Products Standards
McDonald's do? American grain is now used to make American buns to send to the Prairie Provinces where we have the best and the most grain in the world. I have eaten buns made in the United States, Mr. Speaker. They look like they taste, like compressed kleenex. If McDonald's does not like the buns that we make in Regina, Winnipeg or Vancouver, they can damn well go somewhere else to sell their buns. The bun fight is between two corporate empires. What does that accomplish? It picks the pockets of both the farmers and the consumers.
As I said, Canadian flour mills do charge, thanks to the Canadian Wheat Board ensuring a reasonable price to our grain producers-more for flour, in fact, 45 per cent more for flour than the Americans do. A farmer gets only 12 per cent or 13 per cent of the retail price of bread, the rest goes to the middleman.
It is interesting to note that McGavin's is controlled by flour milling companies, 60 per cent owned by Ogilvie Flour Mills- and I want to do a little more research on this but it seems to me that it, in turn, is owned by somebody down south of the forty-ninth parallel-and 40 per cent owned by Maple Leaf Flour Mills, which is in turn, owned by-you guessed it-the CPR.
If the McDonald's clan want to have a feud with the McGavin's clan, they should not be allowed to use bakery workers as cannon fodder.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: What has that got to do with horticulture?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I can tell the hon. gentleman that this is nothing but an additional example of what has been happening. How many fruit and vegetable processing plants since the early 1960s have been shut down in Canada while the processing of that product takes place south of the 49th parallel?
This kind of legislation is as much in the best interests of those who send fruit and vegetable products into Canada as it is in the interests of Canadians, whether they be producers or consumers. It used to be that the farmers, no matter what product they produced, used to deal directly with consumers, or nearly directly, but they have been driven farther apart by separate corporate intervention in the food chain, and the number of hands the food has to pass through between the producers and the consumers keeps increasing. Everybody else takes their bite off the top on the way.
This trans-border ownership of food processing has and will disintegrate the Canadian food system into little branches of regional economies of the United States. From a corporate point of view it makes sense. It makes sense for corporations to consolidate production and trade north and south across the U.S.-Canadian border rather than trade east and west across Canada. Canadian consumers and farmers lose because our traditional ways of dealing with each other are lost in the larger U.S. market.

November 26, 1982
Agricultural Products Standards
The CPR is acquiring running rights over the Rock Island Railway to Kansas City, and through other arrangements can acquire transportation rights all the way to the Gulf of Mexico. The CPR wants higher rates on agricultural products then the CPR can move those goods to the Gulf of Mexico, rather than by way of Vancouver and the St. Lawrence Seaway. Trans-border ownership of food processing causes boom and bust cycles in the regions as the relative cost of production changes. Today it is a flour mill in Toronto-why they are milling wheat in Toronto, I do not know, because they do not grow a bushel of wheat in Toronto-and tomorrow it is in Mississippi. Today it is a packing plant in Calgary; tomorrow it is in California to increase economies of scale for some multinational. This harms our primary producers, processors and the workers in those processing plants here in Canada.
I am not particularly worried about whether some U.S. exporter of fruit and vegetables, or any other agricultural product into Canada, thinks he is getting a good price or not. I am not particularly interested in that. I would be more concerned about seeing to it that agricultural producers in countries that desperately need the business, like Mexico, there in the Caribbean, or those in Central American, get a good price for their product than I would be concerned for the multinational, owned and operated in the United States. If our country allows our farmers to go bankrupt, we will have to pay more for food in the future. It is in our interest to build east-west links rather than wait with supine acquiescence for greater entry of the United States into our markets, while their markets are becoming less penetrable. The U.S. has closed its borders to beef imports from Canada for the rest of this year. So much for that great friendly neighbour and the free trade proponents south of the 49th parallel. The minute Canada becomes more than self sufficient, not only in beef but in any other agricultural product, you will find the forty-ninth parallel closed to Canadian primary producers and processors. Yet we spend time trying to be extra nice to people who send fruit, vegetables and other processed agricultural products into Canada by seeing that they get a fair price. If they are not satisfied with the price, the Government will help them get a preferable one. It has been nothing but a series of governments of both the Liberal and Tory political stripe that have caused the loss of some 400,000 family farms in Canada in the last 25 years. I am not suggesting that all of these farms could have stayed in business, but the policies which have been pursued on prices, production, processing, importing and exporting by successive governments have decreased our family farm population to an all-time low. This has increased our dependency on imported fruits and vegetables and other agricultural products while decreasing our capacity to gain self-sufficiency in Canada.
My colleagues from British Columbia have talked about our failure to become involved in massive greenhouse operations in
order to increase our self-sufficiency, particularly in the production of vegetables. If we will not take advantage of that opportunity, I believe our country should give priority to countries like Mexico and those in Central America for those fruits and vegetables that we import so that we do not have to rely on a multinational corporation which may own supermarkets and wholesale companies in Canada. These multinational companies import their products here and distribute them through their retail outlets at higher costs to the consumers. Sometimes fruits and vegetables which are grown in Canada are processed in the United States and shipped back here. Surely that does not make us worthy of our independence. It is only more of that supine acquiesence that successive old line Party governments have carried on for decades.
The entire costs of those primary producers of fruit, vegetables and grain are being squeezed not only by foreign-owned multinational corporations but by our own corporations as well. Again, Canadian Pacific is squeezing farmers on both their input costs and output costs. Canadian Pacific manufacturers and supplies fertilizers and feeds to farmers. It has a monopoly on the transport of many agricultural products. It is involved in flour milling and retailing. It is involved in meat packing. It is extracting the last possible drop of blood from farmers by giving them the lowest possible prices. All along that production chain, and even at its end, CP charges all that the traffic can bear.
It seems to me that an act to amend the Agricultural Products Standards Act is irrelevant if the farming community is being given to corporations beyond our borders or being handed to agricultural monopolies by default. Government regulations will not require the powerful economic empires to provide high standards of agricultural production because many of those empires, both in Canada and beyond, have more influence on the Government than the regulations. Those companies certainly have more influence than the primary producers do.
In the years that I have been here I have seen producers in the horticultural industry, like the members of the B.C. Fruit Growers and the members of the Niagara Fruit and Vegetable Growers, come here many times to appeal for help, but they lose each time. Nothing has really changed in terms of the health, welfare, good order and growth of the fruit and vegetable industry. Unless and until the Government sets its priorities for an increase of Canadian production and processing in Canada and the expansion of that industry, the situation will not improve.
With respect to those products which we must import during the winter, the Government must give priority to those nations most in need and buy their fruits and vegetables and other agricultural products. Surely that would be more helpful than providing the continuous aid, comfort and protection for corporations outside of our borders which are not interested in the welfare of Canadian producers. They could not care less
November 26, 1982

about what happens to Canadian producers. They can get their products somewhere else.
I return to the matter of the bakery products as an example of what has been happening. The Government, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board in the House, as well as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who is the great defender and protector of Canadian farmers, sat by while a licence was issued for a corporation like McDonald's to import buns made out of American grain into Canada. That is another symptom of the disease that we have seen in our agricultural industry. That is the most recent example. The Minister even pats McDonald's on the back and says that he believes that McDonald's is showing itself to be a responsible corporate citizen in making this decision. I wish he would go to work for McDonald's, preferably south of the 49th parallel.
It is my hope that when this legislation is dealt with in committee Members from all Parties will seriously consider the suggestions made by all those who spoke. Hopefully, a unanimous report will be submitted that recommends the Government introduce other measures to deal with the production and processing of all agricultural products in Canada, by Canadians and for Canadians. I also hope that this report will emphasize carrying on trade with those countries which desparately need exports of those products which we need.
I might remind the House that the same McDonald's Corporation produced a film in tribute to our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Well, I will be darned. What is their slogan?

speechtext: "We do it all for you."

I am simply applying the most recent example of what has happened in international trade concerning buns, and it applies to what has happened before in international trade with Canada in fruit, vegetables and floral products. By the way, I have completed my remarks about buns except for one point. The president of McDonald's, Mr. Cohen, is also one of the top Liberal fund raisers in downtown Toronto. It is passing strange that these things happen. Well, maybe it is not so strange that these kinds of things can happen in the realms of the old line Parties.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) who is not from an agricultural area, I, too, intend to speak briefly on this matter. It is a subject which, although of primary importance to those people who represent agricultural areas, is also interesting to all Members of Parliament. We all have a vested interest in agriculture because we all eat. Unlike the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, it is my intention to obey the rules of relevancy and discuss Bill C-98 which is before us and what that Bill intends to do. It intends to modify or amend Section 6 of the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act. If passed into law, the new Section will read:
No dealer shall engage in the importation into or the exportation from Canada of, or in interprovincial trade in, any agricultural product-

November 26, 1982
Agricultural Products Standards
That is the intention of the Bill. One will not be able to ship blueberries from the Province of Quebec to the Province of Ontario. One will not be able to grow cherries in the Okanagan and ship them into Alberta without having a licence and the authority of the Minister so to do. There might be some reason why one would want to create some impediment to international trade, but having to get the permission of the Government to ship agricultural products from one Province to another in Canada is, in my opinion, detrimental to the interests of the consumers in all Provinces. What we are doing with legislation like this and legislation such as that of the various marketing boards in different Provinces, is to make Canadian agriculture and horticulture inefficient and unable to compete internationally, increasing the final price paid by the Canadian consumer.
This legislation is typical Liberal legislation, when one gets down to reading the fine print. It is very bureaucratic, very arbitrary, and ensures jobs for the boys. In order to regulate interprovincial trade in agricultural products, they will establish a board. This is a favourite trick. They will establish a board under Clause 6.1(1). It will contain not less than three and not more than five members, appointed by the Minister, another five people he can appoint to another one of these boards, and each one of these people will be eligible to serve a term not exceeding five years and will be eligible for reappointment. Anyway, each of these people will serve at the Minister's pleasure.
In how many pieces of legislation have we seen a similar setup where there is a board to be established having judicial powers, to be appointed by the Minister at the Minister's pleasure? I am scared of legislation like this. There might be times when it is reasonable to have it, but everything brought before us seems to contain similar provisions. It is dangerous. We are balkanizing commerce and agricultural products in Canada in establishing these boards, which are creatures of patronage, or can be. The danger is already there. Instead of having competition between producers of horticultural and agricultural products, instead of having proper competition between people engaged in the marketing of those products, we are encouraging these people to compete by hiring lawyers and appearing before the boards to argue their cases, to see who has the lawyer who can present the fanciest argument in legal terms, and they are not competing in a way which would reduce costs and increase efficiency.
Each member of this board is to be paid a significant amount of money authorized by the Treasury Board. That is a standard provision. Because these board members are generalists, very often they are appointed because they happen to be of the same political persuasion and Party as the government in office. That has been known to happen. However, because they are generalists and do not profess to be experts in cherries, cucumbers or some other particular product or method of marketing, the next thing they must do is to form a technical advisory committee. How many times have we seen that
happen? Then, very often, besides having a technical committee, they say that they want input from the consumer and the marketing board, so they set up yet another advisory board to advise the board, which actually possesses quasi-judicial powers. The matter just escalates and gets bigger. More and more people become involved, the matter becomes more and more bureaucratic, and there is more and more difficulty in getting a decision from the board.
Under any reasonable method of operating one of these boards, the decision of the board should be pretty well final in most circumstances. If someone, after having received a decision of the board, thinks that it is not the right decision, or not a point of law, he should be able to appeal it to a court of competent jurisdiction. Under this Act, that will not be the case. Under 6.3(1) we have a new gimmick, a new board called the Review Tribunal, which will be established in a very similar manner. It will consist of people who owe their allegiance to the Minister, having been appointed by him and serving at his pleasure. It is another board to oversee the one established in the Act. It is a gimmick of gimmicks.
1 do not think we need a review tribunal. It is superfluous and will only exist to serve the purposes of the Minister, allowing him to appoint a few more of his friends.
When any Act is introduced into this House by the Liberal Government, the first thing I do is to turn to that section which allows the Government to make regulations. I can guarantee that there is always a section which gives wide-sweeping regulation-making powers. In fact, very often Bills are presented that might as well contain only two clauses, the title and the regulation-making authority.
In the regulatory powers assigned to the Governor in Council under 6.7(1), there is power to prescribe any agricultural product for which a dealer requires a licence. Licences must be renewed annually under 6.7(1). A person must make application for the licence. He should be able to keep that licence unless he has disobeyed the law or there is other good reason to take it away. Of course, that would not employ enough people in the Department of Agriculture or require enough people to sit on these boards. Therefore, each year these people must fill in another group of forms in order to renew their licence.
In paragraph (c) of the regulations, we find something rather frightening. It is left to the Governor in Council to decide the circumstances under which the Minister may suspend or cancel a licence. That is absolute. The Minister will have the power of life and death over somebody whose business it is to deal interprovincially or internationally in agricultural products. There is no use having a board or tribunal supposedly offering some degree of protection to these people because the Minister can have the arbitrary power to take away a
November 26, 1982

licence from someone whose livelihood depends on it. Is there any recourse?
This is typical of the Liberal Government which wants to vest in itself and its democratic right life-and-death power over citizens who should be able to engage in any business they want. There is another favourite. It also prescribes all the records that the licencees have to keep. You can be sure there will be a lot of records and papers to be kept.
At the end we come to the hooker. It is always there. It is the power that gives the Government regulation-making authority over virtually anything. If there is anything not listed here and not covered, they have the regulation-making power under Section 6. They have the power to regulate anything they want.
I do not like this kind of legislation. It strangles commerce, in this case commerce in agricultural-horticultural products. If there is need for standards in agricultural products and a need for these standards to be kept, we can rely on the good graces of the dealers and the inter-relationship between the agricultural product dealers. There is no need for the Government to come in except to establish certain standards.
If a dealer orders Grade A plums and a shipment arrives which is substandard, there is no need for the Minister or any board to become involved. If the dealer receives a substandard product, he will not deal with that supplier for very long. The problem will resolve itself. Alternatively, the dealer can sue in a court of competent jurisdiction. We do not need boards of the type envisaged by this Act.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) is attending the GATT meeting in Europe. He is stating that the nations of the world should try to avoid those things that happened in the thirties when protectionism took over and destroyed trade and commerce throughout the world. Our Secretary of State for External Affairs is saying one thing at the meeting in Europe, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is in this House introducing legislation which will have entirely the opposite effect.
Instead of concentrating on more and more protection, we should be concentrating on ways of becoming more competitive internationally. That would expand rather than contract trade. It would give consumers of agricultural products, which we all are, cheaper and better quality food and would not threaten the livelihood of people in the agricultural industry, as is being done with legislation of this kind.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, May 20, 1981, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-12, respecting bankruptcy and insolvency, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this Bill, I recognize that it is very complex, running a little over 300 pages. Certainly it is going to take a considerable degree of time to get through Committee. There is no doubt that Canadians want a Bill of this nature, but there are certain things that should be taken into consideration in the passage of this Bill. I believe the old bankruptcy Act is about 35 years old, nevertheless if it is going to be 35 years before we get another change to this Bill, so we had better make sure that it is going to do the job for which it was intended.
There are a greater number of bankruptcies now in Canada than ever before. In the depression of the thirties, there were not the number of bankruptcies with which we are now having to cope, simply because in those days credit was not so readily available. Things tightened up, but people were not forced into bankruptcy because they were not carrying the amount of debt that people are carrying today. We have allowed ourselves to get involved in a debt-ridden society, which perhaps started about 20 years ago when money started to free up and more and more of it became available. We got into revolving accounts that revolved over a period of three years, which meant that people were buying things and paying for them over an extended period of three years, things that otherwise they would have saved for and bought at the end of three years. Chargex was introduced, and that further extended the credit. We have witnessed a phenomenon that has never been seen before in Canadian history to the extent that it is today, which is the amount of credit that has been extended to Canadian people, either individually or in businesses.
At the present time there are in Canada about 40 per cent more bankruptcies than there were one year ago. I recognize that during the last quarter of this year this trend has slowed down somewhat, but nevertheless when you consider a 40 per cent increase, I think it is the responsibility of those of us who

November 26, 1982
Bankruptcy
are elected as representatives of the people to make sure that there is legislation in place that is going to protect people.
In the January to October period of 1982, in the farming community, we find that there has been a 50 per cent increase in bankruptcies over last year. Last year there were 230 from January to October, and this year there are 344. One of the unfortunate things is the fact that the Province of Quebec has been hardest hit by this. This point was brought out in the Standing Committee on Agriculture yesterday evening when the Farm Credit people noted that there is an increasing debt load which somebody will have to carry. Possibly it is going to be all of the farmers in the country who are going to have to pick up this extra debt load. West of Ontario there were 53 bankruptcies last year; this year there are 68. That is a 20 per cent increase. Ontario had 123 this year and 126 last year, which means that their bankruptcies are going down this year. Quebec had 145 bankruptcies this year and they had 45 last year, and that is well over a 200 per cent increase. This is in the farming community. Unfortunately these figures do not include all those cases where farmers have just gone out of business, closed their doors, sold their assets and just shut down. There is no way of actually knowing just what that figure might be.
In view of this, I think it tells us, as elected Members of Parliament, that we had better give special attention to the farming community. We have tried to impress upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) that while he was minister of Energy he did untold damage to the agricultural industry by bringing in the National Energy Program in the form that he did, and then putting on the excise tax on energy that is used in the production of food and the operation of the farm. Farmers are big users of energy, and when you consider that somewhere between 28 per cent and 33 per cent of their fuel costs is excise tax going to the federal Government, I think possibly the federal Government had better take notice of that, act accordingly and do something about it.
The Government has to realize that we are living north of the 49th parallel, it is cold, it takes more to heat our businesses and it takes more to heat our homes. It is something that really we cannot do anything about. We are not living in a southern clime where we do not have to worry about that. We recognize that we are in the northern part of the hemisphere, and it is costly to heat our homes. All this adds to our cost of living. When you consider that the same percentages of excise tax apply to the cost of heating our homes as apply to the energy for operation of our farms, that should be looked at.
The Minister of Finance says that he would like to cut down the inflationary aspect. There is nothing more inflationary, Mr. Speaker, than adding absolute costs to our cost of living, such as heating our homes and our businesses. All this adds to the problem that people have in trying to keep their businesses operating. With these extra costs added on, some of them start sinking gradually into the red, and there is no way that they are going to get out. Therefore you have to realize that people
are caught in this dilemma and the Government can do something about it. People are looking for the Government to do something about it in order that this rate of bankruptcies may be lessened. Unfortunately, many people have been misled.
A particular incident I would like to bring to the attention of Hon. Members of the House of Commons that related to our community in Red Deer has to do with a gentleman from Montreal who sold his business and decided that he was going to invest his money somewhere where he thought it was safe. There was an advertisement in the paper from a group of people in Willowdale, Ontario who were making an investment in Alberta, in fact, in my City of Red Deer. He had been told that the place to put his money was in Alberta. These people were investing in a real estate project out there, so he invested his life earnings in that project. Unfortunately either through lack of experience or inflationary costs or for some other reason, the construction of the building was not budgeted properly. Therefore the money that they had borrowed from the lending institution, in this case an insurance company, was not sufficient to complete the facility so it could be put into operation. They could not get funds to complete the project and, as a result of this, the lending institution decided that they were going to move in and foreclose, although the construction was only half completed. The people who initiated the construction could not raise any more money so they lost all they had put into it. Along with that, this gentleman from Montreal, who wanted to put his life savings where it would be protected and he would have a return from it for the rest of his life, lost it all.
It is very sad, Mr. Speaker, that we have this kind of situation. When we deal with a Bill such as C-12, we have to recognize that there should be some kind of protection put into place, if we possibly can, for cases of bankruptcy such as this. There were a lot of subcontractors who lost hundreds of thousands of dollars on this project, too. They had wanted to take over the project from the lending institution to see if they could not put it together, finish it up and thereby get their money out of it. But no, it went down the tubes because the lending institution put it up for tender, somebody thought it was a good thing and grabbed it and paid off the lending institution. They got their money back, but the subcontractors and the fellow from Montreal lost everything. It is a sad situation and we have to recognize this is happening.
Another case in my community is that of farmers who had delivered rapeseed to a processing plant. The plant was expanding and, well, it is a long story but a lot of people recognize the problems of trying to process rapeseed in western Canada in competition with processors in Japan as well as those in eastern Canada. These producers had delivered rapeseed to the plant for processing, and the agreement was
November 26, 1982

that they could sell the rapeseed any time they wanted, at whatever the price was that day. This was their option. They thought it was a good deal, but all of a sudden we find out that the Canada Grain Commission moved in on the processing plant to pick up what they call their letter of credit, or what some people refer to as a bond. In this case, it amounted to $600,000. When we went through the Bank Act, Mr. Speaker, we thought we had protection for those people. When they phoned me about the problem I said, well, we will protect you up to, I think it was $100,000. My good friend, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) knows what I am talking about. We had quite a battle over that in committee, and we thought we had protection for the farmers. However, we found out in order for the farmers to be protected under that section of the Bank Act-my colleague is nodding his head, he agrees with me-the business had to go into bankruptcy. However, in this case the lending institution did not allow that business to go into bankruptcy because they had control of the shares, thereby having total control of the plants' assets. Then we find out that the business itself had apparently been over-valued. It had been assessed at $8 million, but it turns out to be worth probably about $4 million or $5 million. So when you have a bank which has lent $5 million or $6 million and the farmers are owed about $1.25 million, you can understand that there is just not enough to go around.
In any event, the farmers felt that they were protected under this bond worth $600,000. It would at least give them somewhere between 43 cents and 45 cents on the dollar. But what do we find? The bank is now seeking a court order in an attempt to get its hands on the $600,000 as well.
I am not condemning the banks for doing that because they are good business people, they are out to protect their own interests, and you cannot condemn them for that. But somewhere along the line we have to try to provide some protection for producers in our bankruptcy legislation. That is why 1 think this Act deserves a great deal of scrutiny in committee, so that we will come out with the best possible Act that we can, giving as much protection as we can to our producers. There is a feeling in the business community that Bill C-12 is inadequate in so far as receivership is concerned.
There is another area of concern which perhaps relates right back to the earlier example I gave you, Mr. Speaker, where wage earners or subcontractors are not protected. The problems for employees or farmers increased tremendously under receivership as opposed to bankruptcy. When they go into bankruptcy, the are protected. But nevertheless, there always seems to be a way of getting around the problems which seem to surface when these situations develop. I guess possibly it is because the lawyers never cease to do their work and they devise ways and means of advising people how to get around these problems in order to protect their clients. But I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that somewhere along the line the suppliers of merchandise and products of any kind, or the
Capital Gains
working man's wages, should be protected in one form or another.
Another thing I think we have to consider is the sharing of all assets in a bankruptcy so that everyone involved is treated equally. There is another aspect of this Bankruptcy Act which I would like to deal with in relation to the Bank Act. However, I would not like to start today as I think I have only about a minute left. So with that, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could call it four o'clock?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REINTRODUCTION OF MEASURES RESPECTING CAPITAL GAINS TAXATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reintroducing in this Session, the three measures affecting taxation on capital gains, namely, the common stock investment plan changes in the treatment of capital gains, Registered Retirement Savings Plans and the provision for transfer of capital gains on farming assets to RRSPs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure today to introduce this motion with regard to capital gains. At this time in Canada particularly we are finding in the business sector across the country a drying up of capital funds available to the private sector for investment purposes. That is the kind of investment that is needed to get the economy going, particularly in the high-job creation, small business sector.
I should like to focus my remarks now on the plight of the farmer in Canada, Mr. Speaker. Normally, farmers do not contribute to a Registered Retirement Savings Plan. Generally speaking, they put all the money realized from their operation back into the purchase of equipment and making improvements. At least, that was the idea prior to the Government deciding to apply the capital gains tax to farmers. Usually, when a farmer reached the age of retirement he would sell his farm on the open market and use the proceeds as retirement income. In the Prairie communities today, you will find people who have lived all their lives on a farm and built it up to a viable operation, then sold it and moved to town when it came time to retire. As a rule they do not move to Phoenix or California or Hawaii but into places like Biggar, Saskatchewan, Two Hills, Vegreville, Athabasca, Slave Lake or High Prairie, where they live out their days among their friends. The Government has virtually made that an impossible dream.
At present, if a farmer sells his property to his son or daughter, he is charged capital gains tax on the proceeds. I received a letter from a farmer who sold his operation and found that the total capital gains tax payable exceeded the down payment he received. He had built up the farm and

Capital Gains
poured all he could into it, intending to retire and sell it, using the proceeds to buy a house in town for himself and his wife.
The Crosbie budget introduced a measure to provide that $200,000 of the proceeds of the sale of a farm could be rolled into a Registered Retirement Savings Plan, tax free. I submit that is not too much for a farmer to expect, and 1 think it is imperative that the House reconsider that suggestion. We all know the sad tale of the Crosbie budget; the Liberals and the NDP combined to defeat the budget and, as a result, farmers were left out in the cold.
When my NDP colleagues go out seeking the farm vote in the next election, I think they should remind farmers that they are now subject to the capital gains tax because of that Party's action.
In 1980, the Liberals were re-elected on what would appear to be empty promises. They had promised to examine the capital gains tax legislation but all that appeared in the October budget was a promise of a discussion paper on the subject. That paper has not yet appeared, Mr. Speaker, and farmers have not been approached to contribute to it. In November, 1981 there was another budget which further penalized the farmer on the sale of land. Even with all there retreats and flip-flops that appeared in that budget, this measure was not retracted. There is still no relief for farmers.
A search of the records shows that as far back as 1974 the Liberal Government promised relief for farmers by amending the capital gains tax legislation. This has not happened, despite the promises of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the various ministers of finance. Of course, the Minister of Agriculture says that campaign promises do not count! I find that statement unacceptable, Mr. Speaker. I think we must live up to our obligations to the farmers.
It is imperative that we move to bring in legislation that will allow relief from taxes when farmers sell their operations. In some cases, it happens that if a fifth or sixth generation farmer decides to sell to an outsider, he has to pay the accumulated taxes of six generations. That certainly is not right, and I implore Members of the House to adopt the motion which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reintroducing in this Session, the three measures affecting taxation on capital gains, namely, the common stock investment plan changes in the treatment of capital gains, Registered Retirement Savings Plans and the provision for transfer of capital gains on farming assets to RRSPs.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REINTRODUCTION OF MEASURES RESPECTING CAPITAL GAINS TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in the motion put forward by my friend, the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields). He has put his finger on a very important problem. In fact, however, the Government has taken steps to move on this matter. The Lortie Committee called for the establishment of a registered share investment program which would allow capital gains to be paid only on the real gain, as opposed to the total gain which includes the inflationary component; in other words, indexing the value of common shares to make it more attractive for investors to invest in equities.
November 26, 1982
The Hon. Member put his finger on another important problem, the issue of capital gains realized within a RRSP, which are taxed as normal income when they are withdrawn. It seems to me only fair that if we have a capital gains tax which is half the normal tax rate, that the same tax rate be applied to income, be it from a RRSP or from capital gains in the normal sense.
I think the Hon. Member has a very good point. I assure him that those issues have been raised with the Government and with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). I know that on the Registered Share Investment Plan the Lortie Commission recommended that we move ahead with it and that the Minister of Finance indicated that he intended to do so. On the Registered Retirement Savings Plan and the dealing with capital gains there, I am sure it is very logical and I am sure the Minister of Finance will look favourably on it as well. That is my personal opinion, given that we will be introducing RSIPs, which effectively means that only the real gain will be taxed. Basically the same principles are involved as in taxing capital gains out of RRSPs.
There is some relief for farmers if they sell their farms or they are passed from one generation to the next. For example, they have the benefit of what is known as a capital gains reserve for five years, over which time the capital gains can be spread for tax purposes.
During the hearings we had some time ago on income tax matters, the question of capital gains was raised as it relates to family farms and the intergenerational transfer of family farms. In that case farmers who sell or pass land on to one of their children can spread the capital gains tax over a period of up to ten years.
The Hon. Member touched upon some very interesting and some very important points, but we are probably tinkering around the edges of the problem. If we are to talk about capital gains, capital gains tax and how to modify it, it is more important to understand why we have capital gains tax in the first place and, with the present tax structure, why it is essential to have that tax. I think we have to talk about modifications to the tax system, as the Hon. Minister of Finance indicated in the two speeches which he made in the last few days. He dealt with the matter of the complexity of the tax system, which is terribly important, indicated that we need to do something to reduce the complexity. In the Finance Committee yesterday the Minister also indicated that this was especially a problem in the area of small business taxation.
Hon. Members opposite, the Parliamentary Secretary and myself heard about that problem during the month of September when there were hearings into the Income Tax Act and the proposed changes which were put forward in ways and means motions from the November and June budgets. We heard time and again from representatives of the small business community, the tax profession, and the accounting profession that the small business tax system was in total disarray. We heard that small-businessmen could not understand the tax system, and
November 26, 1982

that it was costing them substantial amounts of money. This was also brought to the attention of the Minister. In a speech to the Canadian Tax Foundation the other day he asked its representatives to come forward with recommendations on how the tax system, as it applies to small business, can be greatly simplified to improve the environment for small business people.
Let me say a few things about the tax system, how it got where it is today and how the drive came for capital gains tax. If Hon. Members remember, it came forward during the time of the tax reform in the early 1970s. It was designed to resolve certain types of problems which existed then. With the elimination of capital gains tax today, we would be right back into the situation of having the same problems and of having to find some way to resolve them. Capital gains tax was designed to resolve those problems, and it has resolved them to a great extent. If we are talking about removing capital gains tax and about improving the environment for equity investment, there are other things which must be done as precursors before we can remove or significantly modify capital gains tax.
Let me return to the basic principles of taxation, but especially the income tax system, in the commodity tax, sales tax and income tax systems. On the basis of the income tax system itself, the basic theory behind it underpins our entire structure which is the same as that in the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Japan. That basic theory is that income is generated in the creation of wealth and in the production of goods and services, and that the income generated from the production of goods and services should be taxed somewhere between the time it is created and the time it goes into the consumption stream, or when someone uses it to buy goods and services for consumption purposes. Basically the theory is that it should be taxed somewhere in the line between creation and consumption; that is the basic principle behind taxation.
Mir. Shields: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I draw the attention of the House to the improvement in the Chair, in the person of the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt).

speechtext:
The principle about which we are talking is income being taxed once, not twice. This is the whole basis behind deductions and exemptions in the system. Any moneys expended to earn income, whether it be wages and salaries paid, monies spent for good and services, or raw materials to go into products, are deductible and become taxable income in someone else's hand. The flow of income through the system created by the production of goods or services will be taxed somewhere, in somebody's hands, as it goes from creation to consumption. The whole thing will be subject to tax at some point.
Another fundamental feature of the tax system is the timing of taxation. There has been a great deal of ongoing discussion, and much of the argument about capital gains tax, capital gains reserves, income averaging annuities. Registered Retirement Savings Plans and so on, has revolved around the issue of timing-when do we tax it between the point of creation and
Capital Gains
the point of consumption? There is much dispute as to whether it should be a purely income-based tax system, indicating that as soon as the money is earned it should be taxed. This gives rise to such things as the taxation of accrued income, a very valid and legitimate way of taxing, assuming we want an income-based tax system.
As a general rule in that system we tend to be favouring consumption as opposed to savings and investment. At the other end of the extreme we could have a consumption-based tax system where the income would only be taxed if it were taken out of savings or investments and used for consumption purposes. This specific tax system would be similar to a Registered Retirement Savings Plan-earned money is put into an RRSP and is deductible for tax purposes, but the income from it is not taxed until the money is removed from the plan, presumably for consumption purposes.
They are two extremes. The consumption-based tax system is basically said to favour savings and investment. Thus, tax policy people have a choice. If we want to encourage consumption, we would tend to want an income-based tax system; if we want to encourage savings and investment, we introduce RRSPs, RHOSPs and various kinds of deferral mechanisms to defer taxation, which would move us toward a consumption-based system.
The third basic area about which we must be concerned in taxation is the equity question. There are two kinds of equity with which we have been dealing in our tax system for generations-basically horizontal equity and vertical equity. Horizontal equity is a simple concept-people who make the same amount of money should basically pay the same amount of tax, people who are in the same kinds of circumstances should basically pay the same amount of tax. On the other hand, vertical equity is that as one's disposable income rises one should pay a greater proportion of it in tax. This is the principle which underlies a progressive tax system as opposed to a flat tax system. Progressivity basically came about as a driving force in the tax system in the 1940s just before, during and after the Second World War. That was basically the time when tax systems became steeply progressive under the notion of ability to pay. In other words, those who have the greatest ability to pay should pay more or, under the notion of the marginal utility of income, a dollar to a poor man is worth more in terms of what the economists call utility than is a dollar to a rich person. If you tax a rich person and give the money to the poor person, the over-all utility of the system is more equitable. Those are the basic precepts underlying the notion of progressive taxation, the notion of income tax having a greater reliance on vertical as opposed to horizontal equity.
The other important feature in the tax system is the source of income. Here is where we get into the difficulty which gave rise to the capital gains tax in the first place. The source of income, whether from employment or investment is important. Under an ideal tax system, it would not make any difference

November 26, 1982
Capital Gains
where that income came from. You would treat investment income and employment income exactly the same.
The other hang-up that comes into this area of income source, whether it is employment or investment income, is on the investment side, and that is whether the income is earned by an individual or a corporation. Ideally, you would not tax corporations. Ideally, the income that is earned by a corporation would be attributed to the shareholders and included in their taxable income, subjected to their marginal tax rate. They would pay tax. Corporations would not pay tax.
A great many people say today that corporations really do not pay tax. Corporations either pass the tax along to their shareholders, or to consumers in the form of higher prices. But corporations do not pay tax. Either the owners or the consumers of the products pay tax. People pay taxes. Corporations are legal entities and they do not pay tax. Somebody pays the tax, either the shareholder or the consumer. If you tax the shareholder by putting the income in that person's hand, that is probably the most equitable way to do it.
Over the years, in the United States, here, in Britain, in France, everywhere, we have tended to differentiate between corporations and individuals. If you are an individual, a sole proprietor or a small-business person, and you earn income in your business, it becomes personal income and you are taxed. All of a sudden, a corporation comes along and, for some reason, we think we have to treat that income differently. You could have a three or a four-person corporation. For tax purposes a partnership of four people is treated totally differently than a corporation of four people, although the principles are the same. I own a company, I own it through shares or through a partnership. The income which that company earns is partially mine, represented by the amount of my partnership or represented by the shares I own. There should not be a differentiation, but there is. Then we get into a problem. The biggest problem that has arisen for tax policy is that the corporate tax rate is different from the personal tax rate. Not only that, but we have introduced a small-business tax rate. There is a big-business tax rate and a small-business tax rate. What about an individual, for example, earning income through a corporation, one who is in the 50 per cent tax bracket? If under our present system it were possible for an individual to pass income through a small business corporation and bring it out the other end, the small business corporation, lo and behold, is only taxed at 25 per cent. It may be taxed at only 21 per cent if it were a manufacturing-processing small business. Therefore, an individual, could funnel his income through a corporation and come out the other end paying only 21 per cent or 25 per cent instead of paying 50 per cent. Obviously, tax avoidance could take place, legally, but tax avoidance nonetheless.
Dividends from a corporation to the shareholder have always been taxable. What gave rise to the capital gains tax and the Carter Commission-there would not have been a Carter Commission but for this very problem-is what is called dividend stripping or surplus stripping. In the 1960s it became such a major problem of tax avoidance because
individuals funnelled money through a corporation, and instead of taking dividends on which they would be taxed, they let the dividends and the earnings build up in the corporation, ending up selling the corporation. They took the money as capital gains and the capital gains, of course, were tax free. Therefore, income was being created in the system. Income was going through the system. It was being taken out of the system for consumption and it was not being subjected to tax. That was a fundamental flaw in the tax system.
The principle of plugging that loophole was a capital gains tax. If you take the money out of a corporation as dividends, you pay tax. If you take it out as capital gains, you pay tax, and presumably, through the dividend tax credit mechanism and others, you should get an offset. The corporation now has paid the tax, or you have paid the tax on your income from the corporation, and on your personal income tax form you get a tax credit to offset the fact that you have already paid tax as a part of being an owner of the corporation.
Theoretically, that is the ideal world. The problem is that you have two different corporate tax rates. The dividend tax credit basically offsets only to the level of the small business. If you are a big business paying 50 per cent tax, then you are being taxed twice. At the small-business level you are only being taxed once, theoretically. There are all kinds of problems. But the basic problem we had to face back in the 1960s was this problem of surplus stripping. If you were to eliminate the capital gains tax now or in any major way nullify it, you would wind up with a major tax avoidance problem that could not be tolerated.
There are ways of getting around this problem. However, they involve some fundamental changes to the tax system. For example, we hear people talk about a flat tax. They are talking about a flat tax for a very good reason. Once you take the progressivity out of the tax system, then everybody pays the same rate, and a buck is a buck is a buck and it can be handled that way. If you also apply the flat tax to corporations, then you do not have tax dividends or capital gains. After all, capital gains are simply the present value of future dividends. If I get the money as a person, I pay 30 per cent on it. If the corporation earns the income, the corporation would pay taxes at 30 per cent, let us say, and then the corporation would pass the money to me tax free. But it is not tax free because I own the corporation. The income is flowing to the corporation. It pays the tax and I own the corporation because I am the shareholder, then the money is given to me tax free, or if I earn it some other way, I pay 30 per cent. The same thing applies. It is a nice, clean system. Where the trouble arises, and this is where we are now, is that we have a progressive tax system where individuals have different tax rates than corporations. You can play tax avoidance games by going through corporations to get your income. With a flat tax it does not apply. No matter how I get the income at the corporate level, personally, 30 per cent, or 40 per cent, or whatever the flat tax is, it is paid once. There is no double taxation and the system works very nicely.
November 26, 1982

If we are going to deal with the capital gains tax, it seems to me that we have to deal with capital gains tax in a more fundamental way. We can eliminate the capital gains tax, but it implies some fundamental structural changes to the nature of our income tax system. It means effectively coming to a system where we integrate the personal and the corporate tax system. Right now the small business tax and the personal tax system are, for all intents and purposes, integrated. Tax paid at the corporate level is effectively offset against tax paid personally, so you only pay tax once. For the big corporation, it is not fully integrated, it is under-integrated. The corporation pays tax and the individual pays tax so, to some extent, there is double taxation involved. This has all kinds of implications for equity markets. It has all kinds of implications for equity investment.
As I think the Hon. Member for Athabasca said, one of the reasons why we have so much debt in our capital structure now is probably because of the fact that equity is not relatively attractive for getting money through the debt stream.
Those are the kinds of considerations that we are going to have to take into account if we want to deal with the capital gains tax system. We cannot simply eliminate it because, in the current structure, it would lead to insurmountable problems of tax avoidance which could not be accepted economically or sociably, and I guarantee that it would not be accepted politically.
If we are to deal with the capital gains problem we must deal with the fundamental problems which gave rise to capital gains tax in the first place. I believe that we can do that. There are proposals which can be considered by the House, by the Finance Committee or other committees. I certainly think that we must look at this area very carefully in the future development of the tax system.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REINTRODUCTION OF MEASURES RESPECTING CAPITAL GAINS TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a brief presentation during this debate concerning three measures affecting taxation on capital gains which has been introduced by the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields). The three measures concern the common stock investment plan changes in the treatment of capital gains; the registered retirement savings plan; and the provision of transfer of capital gains on farming assets to RRSPs.
I think the Hon. Member for Athabasca is trying to resurface the Crosbie budget which was defeated on December 11, 1979. I feel obligated to speak in this debate because I think that particular budget is being oversold to a great extent. I do not think it was even really understood by some of the Members in the Conservative Party.
Let me return to some of the original documents from that budget and use some of the Conservative Government's words to describe what it had in mind. One can see that it is not quite how it was portrayed by the Hon. Member for Athabasca, or by Conservative Members from the Prairies.
Capital Gains
I will quote the first aspect of it as it appears in the Budget brief. It says:
Individuals will be encouraged to invest in common stock of Canadian corporations by deferral of capital gains tax on shares purchased through a new Common Stock Investment Plan.
Capital gains was not being eliminated as is often portrayed. It was simply a deferral. As a matter of fact, the plan will probably be discussed before Parliament again because Mr. Lortie, President of the Montreal Stock Exchange, who was involved with one of the groups set up by the former minister of finance, recommended that this particular plan or its variant be discussed. Therefore we will probably see this plan brought back to the House and discussed in the full context of the tax law and philosophy as outlined by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans).
The second point made in the budget note says:
One-half of income earned on common stock investments by Registered Retirement Savings Plans will be exempt from tax when received by individuals on the maturing of their plans.
Apparently, there would have been a reduction in tax for retirement savings plans that are made up of common stocks, under the Crosbie budget.
Since the Hon. Member for Athabasca talked about farms, I will use farms as an example. If the farm which was being disposed of was incorporated, the shareholders would have an avenue to avoid capital gains tax. If it was a normal farm, like the majority, which was privately owned and not incorporated, the third method would have applied. This is the area where I think we are often led down the garden path in rural Canada by some Conservative representatives. What the budget notes actually say and what the budget intendet is:
Farmers will be enabled to get deferral of tax-
I stress deferral of tax. Tax was not eliminated, simply deferred.
-once in a lifetime, on up to $100,000 in taxable capital gains (representing $200,000 of total capital gains) from the sale of their farm by transferring the gains to an RRSP.
Therefore, they were not proposing to do away with part of the capital gains, they were simply proposing to put it into an RRSP and defer the payment of those taxes. The RRSPs that were set up were not made up of common stocks or shares for most farmers but simply transfers of money. The tax was only deferred, not eliminated. This is according to the budget papers that were presented on December 11, 1979.
I believe this is very significant, because that action tells a lot about the Progressive Conservative attitude to farmers with respect to capital gains, much more than do their words.

speechtext: What would you do?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REINTRODUCTION OF MEASURES RESPECTING CAPITAL GAINS TAXATION
speechtext:
Since the Hon. Member asks what we would do, I will point out what some of the NDP provincial Governments have done. I think this is significant, because the collection of capital gains tax is under the authority of both the federal and provincial Governments under the Income Tax

November 26, 1982
Capital Gains
Act. I would draw the Members' attention to the Province of Saskatchewan, which, under an NDP Government, exempted the first $100,000 on capital gains tax on farms. It exempted that tax, it did not defer it. It is one of the few provinces that has done so in spite of all of the provincial Governments being Conservative at one time or another. Provincial Conservative Governments have not addressed the capital gains problem in any real or significant way and not at all in the manner which the Hon. Member for Athabasca would have the House believe. I think we have seen an action which speaks far louder than words.
We believe that this exemption should continue on a federal basis as well. We are prepared to give some reasons for that exemption. We note that the Income Tax Act now exempts home owners and workers in the cities and towns from the capital gain on their principal residence. We say that the reason for the $100,000 exemption on farmland is for similar reasons. It is a form of a retirement investment plan by a farmer or small businessman, similar to the way a large home is for someone who is to retire.
Therefore, we think it is justifiable to provide for an exemption of $100,000 on the first capital gains as it applies to farmers and small businessmen. This would be a much more direct way to attack the problem now. I certainly would agree that revamping the tax system to make it more fair and equitable is desirable and important. It probably should be revamped again due to the changes in the ways taxes are levied in this country.
For your information, Mr. Speaker, I note that in 1952, 53 per cent of the taxes that were collected in this country came from the corporate sector and 46.3 per cent came from individuals. By 1980 that ratio had changed so that 30.5 per cent of the taxes collected in this country came from the corporate sector and almost 70 per cent came from individuals.
We hear much said in the House, particularly from the Official Opposition, about the fact that the country can get back on its feet by removing the Government's involvement in business. I suggest that this has been happening since 1952 in the sense that business has certainly not been paying its share of the capital through taxation in Canada. I understand from some of the remarks of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre that even the Government side recognizes that the tax load does not fall on corporations to the same extent as it falls on individuals. It is inequitable, and is becoming even worse. He did not seem to be giving any indication that that situation will change soon. Until it does change, I think people should expect to gain a few of the perks given to large corporations in the form of tax deferrals.
There is a basic difference between tax deferrals for individuals and for corporations. The main outlet for deferring taxes of individuals is through RRSPs, but individuals eventually need that money. They put it back into income and pay taxes on it. That is not the case with corporate deferrals.
In June of 1980, deferred corporate taxes in this country amounted to something like $20.8 billion. We do not have figures as to how much of those deferred taxes are ultimately paid. We do know that very few of those taxes are actually shown as income and are taxed. We know from studies conducted in the United States concerning deferral of corporate taxes that only about 1.5 per cent of those deferred taxes are actually ever paid. I think the reason is that corporations have an unlimited lifespan. As long as they remain fairly healthy, they can continue to defer their taxes forever, and they never have to declare any of those funds as income and pay taxes on them.
Therefore, I think that the analogy, the rules and the equity, if you like, between individuals and corporations are not fair, and the provisions contained in the Progressive Conservative budget of 1979 were totally unfair for those very reasons. They provided a form of equity to holders of shares or common stocks, but individuals, proprietorships, small businesses or small farms did not get any form of tax write-off, but, rather, only deferrals. I think that was an unfair situation in which to place farmers. It would have been much fairer to simply provide an exemption applicable to the first $100,000 of taxable income, as was done in Saskatchewan. That should have been spread to the federal level and it would have righted a wrong without greatly changing the current tax system.

I would like to refer to capital gains tax. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) gave a very fine speech with many flowery words, in which he very nicely set out the apology always given by the Government. He told of how the capital gains problem grew to the point where the Government began to consider it. My simple question to him,
Capital Gains
though, is, who did all this? Who put it in place? The Carter proposals of 1971, which would have treated a buck as a buck, had quite a bit of support. The Liberal Government did not bring in that report. The bureaucratic proposals which flowed out of the Carter proposals were entirely different. The only people who benefited were the accountants of Canada. The 1971 tax proposals did for the accountants what the constitutional proposals of 1981 will do for those of us who happen to be lawyers. It is like a licence to rob.
I gather the accountants have a huge statue of Mr. Edgar Benson and each year they lay on a new layer of gold leaf because of the enormous fees they have been able to collect as a result of the 1971 amendments. The Canadian Bar Association will soon be putting forth a proposal to put up a similar statue. I think we will put up a statue of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and every year, because of the enormous fees we will receive through fighting these constitutional arguments as a result of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, we will lay on another layer of gold leaf. Over the generations, it will become a tremendous resource for the Canadian Bar Association, so that if we come upon tough times in the future we will be able to take off pieces of this gold and keep our membership up. What the Liberal Party has done has been to help accountants and lawyers.
Let us not forget that we have a motion on the floor to give relief from capital gains tax. The Government obviously has enough members lined up to filibuster this. Once again the Liberal Party is saying to the farmers of this land that they are not prepared to give any relief from capital gains.
Why do we not as a nation exempt bona fide agricultural land from capital gains tax? It is a very small part of our national heritage. This is a huge country, but the amount that is truly arable is a drop in the bucket. When we look at the global scene, the amount of arable land in Canada as a percentage of the world is the smallest fraction. However, out of that smallest fraction, because we put it into the hands of individuals, the farm family, we have produced enough food to export around the world. We have lots.
If we would develop our water resources in the west, we could feed the entire world for generations. We have the land, the solar units and water flowing out of the mountains. If we used it productively, it would be our ace in the hole, and it could turn Canada into the most powerful nation in the world. Within one generation, people are going to be knocking our doors down to get food. We do not need to have agricultural food exporting corporations. They will be banging down the door. Anyone who has looked at the demography figures knows that.
One advantage of exempting just the bona fide agricultural land, all of which is identified, is that it would keep in the small family farms which are clearly more efficient. As the farms get larger, they become more inefficient, the ultimate
