Capital Gains
being the system in China and Russia where they have huge communal farms. We know that production drops off dramatically. In China they are now trying to get back to individual owners. If we exempted bona fide land we would keep more in small family production. That would mean many more tractors, drills and combines which would in turn mean more industrial jobs in Central Ontario. We could keep the enormous strength of that manufacturing industry here in Ontario. It would make it much easier to transfer to the next generation.
The problem with the tax now, as I am sure the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre knows, is that we have a value on the land that was adopted in 1971. We must consider the sale value today. In my part of the country, land sold for about $100 an acre in 1971. It is now selling at about $1,500 an acre, a gain of about $1,400 an acre. Of that, $700 comes into income in the year of sale. For the average 5,000 acre farm, the capital gains tax is truly enormous. A new purchaser coming along can very seldom put up the whole amount at the start. Therefore, the seller has to pay in income tax more money than he receives as the down payment. Not only that, there is nothing left to purchase a small home in the town. It is an enormous problem.
The Liberals talk proudly about the rollover which they have. If the farmer sells it to someone of the next generation who will actually be farming, he can get a rollover. That is true. However, what happens to the farmer with four children, a son living on the land, a son living and working elsewhere and two daughters? He cannot leave it to all of them. What if he wants to leave it to the boy who is on the land because he wants it kept together as an economical farm unit? The farmer wants it to stay together as a family farm.
If it is given to the boy on the farm at the 1971 value, the farmer can get the rollover, but can no longer do fairness and equity to those who left. If it is sold to the boy on the farm at greater than the 1971 value, capital gains tax has to be paid. Once he pays the tax, he does not have enough left to do fairness to the other children. It is a very serious problem which it has come about partly because of inflation.
As a result of these enormous deficits, there is simply too much money chasing too few goods. Inflation tends to settle out. Over the last ten years it settled out on land in particular. In my part of the country, the value of land has increased, not because of its productivity but because of inflation; people in times of inflation trying to put their money into something that will increase in value.
Recently I had an opportunity to buy some land. I ran calculations based on its productivity. Based on productivity, the land should have been $200 an acre, yet people are paying $700, $800, up to $1,000 to try to protect themselves from future inflation. Honest people trying to expand simply cannot pay that much, because productivity indicates it is only worth $200. This is a serious problem. As a result, we find foreign money being used to buy up land. Larger corporations with enormous cash flow from sources other than agriculture are purchasing the land. It is therefore becoming more inefficient. We are losing the family farms, the small communities and the
manufacturing industries which produce tractors and other kinds of equipment. Instead, huge four-wheel drive units that are produced in the United States and elsewhere are being bought.
The net result of that capital gains tax exemption for bona fide land would be cheaper food. My friend from Ottawa Centre pointed out that the capital gains would catch speculators. That is true, but there is a very little genuine speculation on bona fide agricultural land. If the tax were attached only to the land, and it became a city subdivision, fine, tax it to death. However, the fact that there would be an exemption on bona fide land would tend to keep land for agricultural purposes. As I said earlier, that is what we need for the future. There is no doubt that the rest of the world is in deep trouble in terms of food production.
It has always been a source of great sadness that Canadians, one-half of 1 per cent of the world population sitting on the resources of half this continent, are out in the world capital markets, down on both knees with their hats off, begging the world to lend us money. At the same time we are competing with the Third World countries for oil. Why should we do that? We do not want to compete with them for oil. We should be a source of capital to the world and a source of energy, yet we are not.
It is close to five o'clock. I hope the House will accept this motion of my hon. friend for Athabasca (Mr. Shields).

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words at the end of what I have found to be a very interesting discussion. I am sorry that the mover of the motion was not able to stay because I wanted to ask him a question. Perhaps the honourable Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) can give us some information.
By my calculations, under the new proposals for the treatment of capital gains, proposals developed from the November budget, it looks as if in the worst possible case a taxpayer, given the reserves and the rates of taxation, will have to pay 5 per cent of the gain per annum over a five-year period. If a farmer sells his farm outside his family, he would then pay 5 per cent of that gain for a five-year period and discharge all his responsibilities for his capital gain. If he sells his farm to one of his sons or to someone in his immediate family, the reserve period is stretched out for ten years. Therefore, his liability is only 2.5 per cent of the gain per annum. That does not seem to be an onerous problem, and those are the worst figures without any allowance for forward-averaging or any of the other normal deductions the farmer might be able to take into account.
We hear stories about these difficulties, but I wonder if the Hon. Member could explain to me, perhaps privately, how 5 per cent of the gain or, in the case of a family sale, 7.5 per cent of the gain per annum, is really that onerous?
